Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

An activation map is built from **local activation times** (LATs). Each LAT is an annotated time on a local
electrogram minus the time of a **reference** electrogram on the same beat. Errors in the reference cancel between
points recorded on one beat but add between points recorded on different beats. The annotation rule matters. In the
m03 model, the unipolar **steepest downstroke** falls when the front passes the electrode, and the bipolar **peak**
when it passes the bipole midpoint, as long as the spacing is small enough. An **onset** rule fires earlier, by an
amount that grows with the electrode's height above the tissue. Noise moves a threshold crossing by noise divided by
slope. In a reentry every site activates once per cycle, so the **window of interest** picks which copy to show; where
it wraps, earliest meets latest. **Far-field** deflections are broad, so their slope-to-amplitude ratio is small. They
can be subtracted with a template or blanked by time, at a price.

## From the field

- **The window is set from a fixed reference.** An early description of magnetic electroanatomic mapping set a window
  of electrical interest from a stable reference electrogram, usually in the coronary sinus or atrial appendage, wide
  enough to include atrial activation before P-wave onset [@marchlinski1998].
- **Window and reference errors spoil reentry maps.** Reviewing 43 maps of atrial tachycardia from 14 patients, one
  group traced poor maps to a window shorter than the cycle length, less than 95% of the cycle mapped, cycle-length
  variability or an unstable reference, among other causes [@koawing2015].
- **Far-field signals are common and shaped by anatomy.** After pulmonary vein isolation, far-field signals from the
  superior vena cava appeared in the right superior vein in 35 of 92 patients, with amplitude 0.24 ± 0.11 mV and a
  sharper main deflection than far-field left atrial signals [@gu2022].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $t_i$ annotated local time; $t_{\mathrm{ref}}$ reference time; $\sigma_a$, $\sigma_r$
annotation and reference SDs; $U$ unipolar potential; $A$ its strength; $s$ front distance; $c$ conduction velocity;
$a = w + h$ front width plus electrode height (m03); $B$ bipolar potential; $d$ spacing; $\theta$ angle between the
bipole axis and propagation; $t_{\mathrm{mid}}$ time the front reaches the bipole midpoint; $f$ onset fraction;
$\sigma_n$ noise SD; $x$ a signal; $T$ cycle length; $w_0$, $W$ window start and width; $l$ local signal; $\phi$
far-field template; $g$ its gain.

### Reference and LAT

$$
\mathrm{LAT}_i = t_i - t_{\mathrm{ref}}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\mathrm{LAT}_i - \mathrm{LAT}_j) = 2\sigma_a^2 + \begin{cases} 0 & \text{same beat} \\ 2\sigma_r^2 & \text{different beats} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-m22-lat}

A reference that shifts from beat to beat adds its error to every point collected one beat at a time. In the lab, with
an illustrative 0.5-ms annotation error and 3-ms reference error, a plane front fitted to 10 points from one beat had an
interquartile range of speed error of 0.04 m/s; spread over 10 beats it was 0.24 m/s (lab part A). Conduction velocity
methods are the subject of m25 [@cantwell2015].

### Annotation rules

For the m03 model $U = As/(s^2 + a^2)$ with $s = -c(t - t_0)$, and a bipole along the propagation direction:

$$
\frac{dU}{ds} = A\frac{a^2 - s^2}{(s^2 + a^2)^2} \text{ is largest at } s = 0, \qquad B(t_{\mathrm{mid}} + \tau) = B(t_{\mathrm{mid}} - \tau), \quad \lvert B\rvert \text{ peaks at } t_{\mathrm{mid}} \text{ if } d\cos\theta < 2\sqrt3\,a
$$ {#eq-m22-intrinsic}

So the unipolar steepest downstroke marks when the front reaches the electrode. This matches the theory and ideal
simulations of Steinhaus, who also found differences above 1.8 ms under nonideal conditions [@steinhaus1989]. The
bipolar signal is symmetric about the midpoint activation. Its peak sits there while the spacing is below the limit;
beyond it the peak splits in two (lab part B). An **onset** rule fires earlier. In the small-spacing limit:

$$
t_{\mathrm{mid}} - t_{\mathrm{on}} = \frac{a}{c}\sqrt{x_f}, \qquad \frac{1 - x_f}{(1 + x_f)^2} = f
$$ {#eq-m22-onset}

For $f = 0.1$, $\sqrt{x_f} = 0.84$. With a 2-mm bipole the onset led the midpoint activation by 1.2 ms at 0.5 mm height
and 2.9 ms at 3 mm (lab part B). Height changes with contact, so onset LATs carry a bias that varies from point to
point.

::: {.demo #m22-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m22-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m22-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m22-d1-rules.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the m03 arctangent front, a planar front along the bipole axis; steepest downstroke, peak and onset found on the
  closed-form traces (@eq-m22-intrinsic, @eq-m22-onset). Tested against `epml.annotation`.
- Parameters: conduction velocity 1.0 m/s [@heil2023]; front width 0.3 mm (m03); default height 1 mm [@riccio2021] and
  spacing 2 mm [@iafdb], as in m03; onset fraction adjustable.
- What it ignores: noise, filtering (m04), wavefront curvature, oblique incidence, and tissue that is not uniform.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Peak and steepest downstroke are unbiased in the ideal model; onset is biased by height.
- Wide spacing relative to height splits the bipolar peak.

### Noise

$$
\sigma_t = \frac{\sigma_n}{\lvert x'(t_c)\rvert}
$$ {#eq-m22-jitter}

A threshold crossing at $t_c$ moves by the noise divided by the slope there. In the lab, with noise at 2% of the
bipolar peak-to-peak, the onset moved by 0.036 ms as predicted, the peak by 0.11 ms and the unipolar steepest
downstroke by 0.20 ms. At 5% the steepest downstroke sometimes locked onto noise, with an SD of 6.4 ms (lab part C).
Derivatives amplify fast noise.

### Window of interest

$$
\mathrm{LAT}_W = w_0 + \bigl((t - t_{\mathrm{ref}} - w_0) \bmod T\bigr), \quad \text{kept only if } \mathrm{LAT}_W < w_0 + W
$$ {#eq-m22-woi}

In a reentry each site activates once per cycle, so its time after the reference is defined only up to whole cycles.
The window picks one copy. Where it wraps, the earliest and latest sites sit side by side ("early meets late"), and
moving the window moves that line. A window shorter than the cycle leaves part of the circuit out: in the lab a 200-ms
window on a 250-ms cycle annotated 80% of the circuit (lab part D). This is why a window shorter than the cycle length
spoiled reentry maps [@koawing2015].

::: {.demo #m22-d2 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m22-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m22-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m22-d2-window.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: an idealized macroreentry with constant speed around the circuit, a stable cycle length and a fixed
  reference (@eq-m22-woi). Tested against `epml.annotation`.
- Parameters: cycle length (default 250 ms), window start and width are illustrative and adjustable; the reference
  sits at a fixed point of the circuit.
- What it ignores: cycle-length variability, bystander regions and dead-end pathways, slow zones, and annotation error.
:::

### Far-field rejection

$$
\frac{\max\lvert dU/dt\rvert}{\operatorname{pp}(U)} = \frac{c}{a}, \qquad x = l + g\phi \;\Rightarrow\; \hat g = \frac{\langle x, \phi\rangle}{\langle \phi, \phi\rangle} = g + \frac{\langle l, \phi\rangle}{\langle \phi, \phi\rangle}
$$ {#eq-m22-farfield}

Signals from distant tissue are broad: their slope-to-amplitude ratio falls with distance. In the lab a local signal at
1.3 mm had a ratio of 0.77 per ms, an illustrative far-field deflection 0.08 per ms. When the far-field shape is known
up to a gain, least squares can subtract it; the gain absorbs any local signal that overlaps the template. A small local
signal annotated on the far field before subtraction and correctly after it, while blanking around the far-field time
would have discarded a local activation 10 ms away (lab part E). One clinical study cancelled far-field signals from
unipolar recordings by least squares, which lowered unipolar voltage by about 25% [@ragot2021]. Simulations show that
far-field contributions grow as the electrode moves away from the tissue, and remain even in contact
[@martinezmateu2019].

**Key takeaways**

- Sharpness separates near from far; overlap in time defeats both blanking and subtraction.
- A far-field template must not contain the local signal you want.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Every activation map depends on the reference, the window and the annotation rule.
Reentry maps need a window close to the cycle length and a stable reference [@koawing2015]. The window is usually
anchored to a stable electrogram [@marchlinski1998]. Far-field signals from neighboring structures can resemble local
activity [@gu2022], and removing them changes what a unipolar voltage map shows [@ragot2021].

**What the evidence is.** Simulation [@steinhaus1989; @martinezmateu2019], a retrospective review of tachycardia maps
[@koawing2015], clinical observational studies [@gu2022; @ragot2021] and a method review [@cantwell2015].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **What was the reference, and was it stable?** (@eq-m22-lat)
- **Which annotation rule, and could the electrode height vary?** (@eq-m22-intrinsic, @eq-m22-onset)
- **Did the window cover the cycle?** (@eq-m22-woi)
- **How were far-field signals handled?** (@eq-m22-farfield)

## How experts think

Before trusting an activation map, ask:

1. **Is the reference stable from beat to beat?** (@eq-m22-lat)
2. **Which rule annotated the points, and does it depend on contact?** (@eq-m22-intrinsic, @eq-m22-onset)
3. **How noisy were the signals, and how steep at the annotation?** (@eq-m22-jitter)
4. **Does the window cover the whole cycle, and where does it wrap?** (@eq-m22-woi)
5. **Could any annotation be on a far-field signal?** (@eq-m22-farfield)

One sentence to keep: **a LAT is a choice of reference, window and rule, not a measurement of the heart alone.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| LAT (@eq-m22-lat) | $t_i - t_{\mathrm{ref}}$; difference variance $2\sigma_a^2$ in one beat, $+2\sigma_r^2$ across beats |
| Rules (@eq-m22-intrinsic) | steepest downstroke at $s = 0$; bipolar peak at midpoint if $d\cos\theta < 2\sqrt3\,a$ |
| Onset (@eq-m22-onset) | leads by $(a/c)\sqrt{x_f}$; $(1 - x_f)/(1 + x_f)^2 = f$ |
| Noise (@eq-m22-jitter) | $\sigma_t = \sigma_n/\lvert x'\rvert$ |
| Window (@eq-m22-woi) | $w_0 + ((t - w_0) \bmod T)$, kept if $< w_0 + W$ |
| Far field (@eq-m22-farfield) | sharpness $c/a$; $\hat g = g + \langle l, \phi\rangle/\langle\phi, \phi\rangle$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Window from a fixed CS or appendage reference | @marchlinski1998 |
| 43 maps, 14 patients; window < cycle, < 95% mapped, unstable reference among causes of poor maps | @koawing2015 |
| Far-field SVC signals in 35/92 patients; 0.24 ± 0.11 mV | @gu2022 |
| Unipolar voltage about 25% lower after far-field cancellation; 12 patients | @ragot2021 |
| Activation-time differences above 1.8 ms under nonideal conditions (simulation) | @steinhaus1989 |
| Conduction velocity 1.0 m/s; height 1 mm; spacing 2 mm | @heil2023, @riccio2021, @iafdb |
| Noise levels, reference jitter, cycle length, far-field shape | illustrative |
| Onset leads, jitters, window coverage, gains | our own code |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Define local activation time.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The annotated time on the local electrogram minus the annotated time on a reference electrogram in the same
beat (@eq-m22-lat).

</details>

**Q2. Why does a multielectrode catheter give better local conduction-velocity estimates than single points from
different beats?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Points from one beat share the reference error, which cancels in their differences; points from different beats each
carry their own (@eq-m22-lat).

</details>

**Q3. Why is the unipolar steepest downstroke used as the activation time?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In theory and ideal simulation it coincides with the fastest upstroke of the local action potential, the moment the
front passes (@eq-m22-intrinsic) [@steinhaus1989].

</details>

**Q4. When does the bipolar peak mark the midpoint activation, and when not?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In the m03 model, when $d\cos\theta < 2\sqrt3\,a$; with wider spacing relative to height the peak splits into
two (@eq-m22-intrinsic).

</details>

**Q5. What bias does an onset rule introduce?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It fires before the front arrives, by $(a/c)\sqrt{x_f}$ in the small-spacing limit, so the bias grows with electrode
height and falls with conduction velocity (@eq-m22-onset).

</details>

**Q6. How does noise affect a threshold-crossing annotation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It moves it by noise SD over the slope at the crossing (@eq-m22-jitter).

</details>

**Q7. Why can the steepest-downstroke rule fail badly on noisy signals?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It uses a derivative, which amplifies fast noise; a noise spike can have a steeper slope than the true
downstroke (@eq-m22-jitter).

</details>

**Q8. What does the window of interest do in a reentry?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It chooses which cycle's copy of each activation to show, by wrapping times modulo the cycle length into the
window (@eq-m22-woi).

</details>

**Q9. What happens if the window is shorter than the cycle length?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Part of the circuit is not annotated or is assigned to the wrong cycle (@eq-m22-woi); this was among the causes of poor
reentry maps in one review [@koawing2015].

</details>

**Q10. How can you tell a far-field deflection from a local one?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Far-field signals are broad, with a small slope-to-amplitude ratio (@eq-m22-farfield); timing relative to the far-field
source is another clue.

</details>

**Q11. What is the risk of subtracting a far-field template?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

If local activity overlaps the template, the fitted gain absorbs part of it (@eq-m22-farfield) [@ragot2021].

</details>

**Q12. What is the risk of blanking?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Any local activation inside the blanked span is lost (@eq-m22-farfield).

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. Annotation SD 1 ms, reference SD 2 ms. SD of a LAT difference across two beats?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\sqrt{2 + 8} \approx$ 3.2 ms (@eq-m22-lat).

</details>

**S2. The same two points recorded on one beat?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\sqrt2 \approx$ 1.4 ms (@eq-m22-lat).

</details>

**S3. $a$ = 1 mm. Largest bipolar spacing (along the propagation direction) that keeps the peak at the midpoint?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$2\sqrt3 \approx$ 3.5 mm (@eq-m22-intrinsic).

</details>

**S4. Noise 0.02 mV, slope 0.5 mV/ms at the crossing. Timing SD?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.04 ms (@eq-m22-jitter).

</details>

**S5. Cycle 300 ms, window −200 to 100 ms. A site activates 150 ms after the reference. Assigned LAT?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

−150 ms (150 − 300) (@eq-m22-woi).

</details>

**S6. Speed 1 mm/ms, $a$ = 2 mm. Slope-to-amplitude ratio of the unipolar signal?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.5 per ms (@eq-m22-farfield).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Activation times from electrograms.** Steinhaus's comparisons of electrogram and action-potential timing in
  simulated cables [@steinhaus1989]. This module: annotation rules.
- **Map grading and its pitfalls.** Koa-Wing and colleagues' examples of poor maps from window and reference
  settings [@koawing2015]. This module: window of interest.
- **Far-field cancellation.** Ragot and colleagues' unipolar recordings before and after cancellation [@ragot2021].
  This module: far-field rejection.

## Further reading

- **Methods.** A review of LAT annotation and conduction-velocity algorithms [@cantwell2015].
- **Reading maps.** A tutorial review of what activation-map colors mean [@delcarpio2010].
- **Far field.** Simulation of far-field contributions [@martinezmateu2019]; clinical far-field signals [@gu2022].
- **Related modules.** m03 (electrograms), m04 (recording chain), m11 (EP study), m24 (activation maps), m25
  (conduction velocity), m26 (map uncertainty).
